title: Bounce-Back Candidates
brief: Which players had a down season from injury, role or a shooting or steals slump and could return to their earlier level? It must explain why one bad season should not set the price and which bounce-backs depend on unstable stats.
summary: Do not price a player off one bad season. If a player lost last season to injury, a lost role or a free throw slump, he is often too cheap now, so bid into the expert ranges rather than the depressed market price. Bounce-backs that rest on steals, field goal percentage or three-point percentage are less certain. Pay less for them, put them in builds that can absorb a miss, and use the first weeks to confirm the recovery.

sections.heading: One bad season should not set the price

paragraphs.text: The experts agree on the core rule. One bad season does not make a player bad. A down year also should not flip a long-term story, such as a player being reliable. Elite skills like steals tend to snap back after a down year, like an elastic band. In our auction, set your price from the expert range for this season. Do not use last season's box score, and do not use what our league paid last October.

The market often overreacts. Dyson Daniels is the clearest case. His Yahoo average cost has collapsed after a down year, but the experts still see a round 3 to 4 value and expect him to go above 20 USD. If you want him, be ready to bid into that range. Waiting for the market price will probably not get him.

Drafters are also too scared of players coming back from injuries that cost them last season. You can be more confident than their ADPs suggest. This applies to Jayson Tatum after the Achilles, Jalen Williams after wrist and hamstring injuries, Domantas Sabonis after an injury-hit season and Jakob Poeltl with a healthy back. Do not overcorrect, though. One clean or one injured season should not rewrite a long injury history in either direction.

sections.heading: Where a down year comes from

paragraphs.text: Bounce-back candidates come from three sources: role changes, injuries and shooting slumps. Sort each candidate by source before you bid. The source tells you what to check in the first weeks.

Role cases depend on minutes. Trae Young needs 33 or more minutes. Zach LaVine needs to keep starting with 30 or more minutes. John Collins needs 30 to 31 minutes. Myles Turner needs close to 30 minutes under a new coach, and Ivica Zubac needs more than 30 minutes against Huff. If the minutes are not there early, the bounce-back is not happening. Cut late flyers rather than wait.

Efficiency can also recover when a player's usage is reduced. Aaron Nesmith's case rests on his FG% getting back from 41% toward 48 to 50% with Haliburton back. Track his FG% and his starting spot on waivers rather than paying for the recovery in advance.

Big free throw drops with no clear reason are a pattern that likely reverts. This makes FT% the safest stat to bet on. It supports Coby White and Jalen Green, whose FT% is expected to recover. The data flags Evan Mobley's FT% recovery as uncertain, so do not build his price on it. Value him as a punt FT% piece.

Steals swing in both directions. A player whose steals dropped can bounce back, but never pay for a career-high steal rate. Daniels is a steals bounce-back, so check in the first weeks that he stays above two steals per game.

FG% and 3P% slumps are the least certain bounce-backs on this list. Tatum's rim finishing, Bam Adebayo's shooting, Derrick White's FG% and Turner's FG% all have to recover. Most of these players fit punt FG% builds. If you roster several of them, punting FG% means a failed recovery costs you nothing. If you keep FG%, pay toward the low end of their ranges.

The notes split on three names. On Zubac, one side tags him a bounce-back, but Josh doubts a return to top 30 form, and the experts cap him at about 14 USD. On Turner, one side blames his poor 2025-26 on Doc Rivers and expects a rebound under a new coach. The other side calls him fine around picks 100 to 120 but not as a top 90 pick. On Christian Braun, Moore predicts a bounce-back, while a newer note expects a better finish and still does not buy him. In each case, bid the cautious side's price. You then capture the upside without paying for it.

sections.heading: How to use this in our league

paragraphs.text: Our auction drafts 144 players, so the stage of the draft matters. Buy the core injury and role cases at their expert ranges in the early and middle rounds. Take the cheap flyers (Coby White, LaVine, Collins, Green, Poeltl, Turner) at 1 to 5 USD late, where a miss costs almost nothing. Leave Braun and Nesmith on waivers, or take them only as 1 USD last picks, and watch their early box scores with FAB ready.

Check the playoff schedule before you pay full price. Miami has only 10 games in our playoff weeks, Indiana plays 3, 4 and 3 games, and Cleveland has a 2-game finals week. A bounce-back that arrives can still be sold to another manager before the 2027-03-04 trade deadline if his team's playoff schedule is weak.
